extracted.intended_audience: writers, game designers, students and scholars of narrative/story structure interested in East Asian four-act technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for using the East Asian four-part narrative structure (ki/shō/ten/ketsu) in stories, poems, arguments, games, and other media; explains each act's function, regional variants, and practical notes on pacing and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-part structure (ki/shō/ten/ketsu)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kishōtenketsu describes the four-part structure of many classic Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese narratives. The parts can be summarized as: introduction, development, twist or reversal, and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core organizing principle: stories built with these four acts deliberately place a turning point in the third act and resolve in the fourth. Use the four parts as distinct sections (they can be as short as a sentence or as long as a chapter) and treat the third part as the key shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ki (起) — Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Ki / 起: start or introduction, usually meaning the reason a thing begins; in a story this is an introduction to the characters, era, and other information required to understand the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Ki to set up setting, characters, and necessary background without initiating the central turn or climax. Keep it focused on what readers need to understand what follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shō (承) — Development
rubrics_metrics.description: Shō / 承: development — follows leads towards the twist in the story; no major changes so far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the situation, deepen detail, and build expectations toward the twist. In some regional descriptions (Korean '승') this can be the beginning of action without necessarily solving a problem — often a movement toward self-realization rather than conflict resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten (転) — Twist / Turning point
rubrics_metrics.description: Ten / 転: turn, turning point, crescendo — the story turns toward an unexpected development. This is the crux of the story, the yama (ヤマ) or climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold back a major story element until this third act; the twist often changes the genre or reframes prior material. There can be several turns, but the third of four acts is typically the biggest. The 'twist' need not be dramatic conflict; it can be surprising reframing, irony, or tonal shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ketsu (結) — Conclusion / Resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Ketsu / 結: result — conclusion that wraps up the story; also called ochi (落ち) or ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve or show the consequence of the twist. "The conclusion is said to need to be quick and one should not linger long on that part of the essay." Use Ketsu to provide closure, reflection, or the lesson gained from the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-conflict-centeredness (structure 'without conflict')
rubrics_metrics.description: Kishōtenketsu as a narrative structure does not center on conflict as part of its structure, especially when compared to common Western narrative structures like the three-act structure and Joseph Campbell's 'Hero's Journey.' It has been popularly described as 'without conflict,' although narratives created using kishōtenketsu can and often do contain conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using kishōtenketsu, emphasize juxtaposition, revelation, and tonal/semantic shift rather than building toward a conflict-driven climax. Avoid forcing a Western-style conflict if following this pattern, but recognize conflict can still appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold back major element until the third act (genre-shifting twist)
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure deliberately holds back a major story element until the third of four acts, which often changes the genre of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan your narrative so that a significant piece of information, perspective, or event is withheld until Ten, enabling re-interpretation of earlier material. This is a key stylistic/structural device of kishōtenketsu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition length and form flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitions can be anything from a sentence to a full paragraph which contrasts with e.g. the five-paragraph essay where one sentence is encouraged for all transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be flexible with how much space you devote to connecting acts—use short or extended transitions as suits tone and medium. You may also set up callbacks to the beginning of the piece during transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/applicability across media and units
rubrics_metrics.description: This structure can be used in yonkoma manga, documents, dissertations, music, sentences, chapters, and even clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply kishōtenketsu at multiple scales: a four-line poem maps naturally; a four-panel comic can map panels to ki/shō/ten/ketsu; a chapter or essay can follow the same arc. Adapt the granularity to your medium and pacing needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use as argumentative or expository framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The same pattern is used for arguments (example: discussion about the usage of photocopying machines analyzed into Introduction, Development, Twist, Conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When structuring an argument or explanatory piece, use Ki to introduce the topic, Shō to develop it, Ten to introduce a counterintuitive comparison or caveat (the twist), and Ketsu to resolve and draw implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional/linguistic variations and nuanced functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations exist by region (Chinese qǐchéngzhuǎnhé, Korean giseungjeongyeol, Vietnamese khai-thừa-chuyển-hợp) and the character meanings emphasize different nuances (e.g., Chinese: qǐ=start, chéng=handling/process, zhuǎn=turn, hé=result).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting the form, consider cultural/linguistic variants: for poetry the line-to-function mapping differs; Korean descriptions emphasize self-realization in 승; Chinese poetic lineage ties to specific four-line forms. Use local conventions when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic four-line composition mapping (qijue / tứ tuyệt)
rubrics_metrics.description: In classical Chinese and Vietnamese poetry the four-line form (qijue / tứ tuyệt) maps to qi/cheng/zhuan/he: line 1 introduces, line 2 expands, line 3 turns, line 4 concludes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing short-form poetry in this tradition, allocate each line a function: introduce an image or idea, expand its emotional/imagistic flow, deliver a turn or shift (often surprising), and conclude by resolving or offering reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Game/design application: level and mechanic pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept has been used in game design (notably by Nintendo designers) to structure levels and design elements following kishōtenketsu principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers can introduce mechanics/setting (Ki), develop and explore them (Shō), present a surprising twist or novel use (Ten), and resolve or provide payoff (Ketsu). Use the twist to reframe prior play and create delight without relying solely on conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive and instructional effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies found that students familiar with this structure were better able to pick out the main points of essays written in this form; the structure may organize cognitive thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the effectiveness of a kishōtenketsu piece, consider whether the form helped readers identify main points or organize understanding; adapt teaching/writing to readers' familiarity with the form.
